title: What the record said last month, under the same gate as today
summary: History is the same personal data, one generation older - so reading it costs the same purpose, the same consent and the same audit record as reading the current value. And it dies with the person, in the same transaction.

steps.label: A person with a tier
steps.note: Versioning is off by default: history extends the storage-limitation clock, so switching it on is a deliberate act. This stack has SUNDER_VERSIONS_KEEP set.

steps.label: The tier changes
steps.note: Re-registering the same identifiers merges into the same person's blob. The value that is about to be overwritten is snapshotted first, inside the same transaction - history cannot miss a generation nor record one that never landed.

steps.label: And changes again
steps.note: Two overwrites, so there are two prior generations to ask about.

steps.label: The current value is gold
steps.note: The ordinary read path, for contrast.

steps.label: List the versions
steps.note: Metadata only: which generation, written by whom, when. This listing is itself an audited read - asking what history exists is a disclosure about the person.

steps.label: Read version 1 without a purpose: refused
steps.note: The gate does not weaken with age. No purpose, no answer.

steps.label: With a purpose, the old value comes back
steps.note: Bronze - what the record said before the first change. Purpose, consent, the attribute allowlist, scope and the tombstone check all ran, and the audit row was written BEFORE the value was released.

steps.label: Erase the person
steps.note: The interesting question for history is what Article 17 does to it.

steps.label: History died with them
steps.note: Not pruned later by a sweep - deleted in the erasure transaction. History that outlived erasure would be the loudest possible way to fail Article 17.
